title: Carlton Barrett - Wikipedia
notes: Born 17 December 1950, Kingston, second son of Wilfred and Violet Barrett; 'Carly' and 'Field Marshal'; a first drum set 'from empty paint cans he found on the street'; 'heavily influenced by Lloyd Knibb' of the Skatalites; contemporaries Sly Dunbar, Leroy 'Horsemouth' Wallace, Style Scott, Carlton 'Santa' Davis; the Soul Mates, the Rhythm Force, then the Hippy Boys (Max Romeo, Leroy Brown, Delano Stewart, Glen Adams, Alva Lewis) with his brother; joined the Wailers in 1969; 'a highly syncopated, broken triplet pattern on the hi-hat'; 'dazzling drum introductions'; credited with popularising the one drop; Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Drummers (2016); on Bunny Wailer's Blackheart Man, Augustus Pablo's King Tubbys Meets Rockers Uptown, Peter Tosh's Legalize It and Equal Rights; shot dead outside his home at 12 Bridgemount Park Avenue, Kingston, on 17 April 1987, aged 36; his widow Albertine and two men were sentenced in 1991. The page carries a citation-needed tag.

title: One drop rhythm - Wikipedia
notes: 'popularized by Carlton Barrett'; 'the creator is disputed' between Carlton Barrett, Aston Barrett and Winston Grennan (the Guardian: Grennan 'developed for rock steady the one-drop rhythm'); the snare (usually a cross-stick) and bass drum together on beat three, beat one empty; rockers puts the bass drum on every quarter, steppers on every eighth; Legend's one-drop songs (No Woman, No Cry, Three Little Birds, Get Up, Stand Up, Waiting in Vain, Stir It Up, One Love, I Shot the Sheriff) and its steppers songs (Is This Love, Exodus, Buffalo Soldier, Satisfy My Soul, Jamming).

title: Robert Santelli, 'The Reggae Drummers', Modern Drummer, July 1983 (issue 45), pp. 18-20 and 82
notes: Read in the archive.org scan's text (md45cs_djvu.txt). Interviews with Sly Dunbar, Carly Barrett, Nelson Miller, Skyjuice and Horsemouth Wallace. Santelli: 'the exceptionally tightfisted drumming of brother Carly'. Barrett: 'Fams and I, we always had a special pattern for playing, a cool drive that everybody take notice of'; 'it's a spiritual vibe that I try and get from my drums to the music. Because drums come from the slavery days and from Africa ... The reggae drummer carries that history'; 'Bob never interfere with his musicians. He always leave the basic parts for his musicians to figure out'; his best drumming: 'I think it Kaya ... So I got to play deep; more within'; before the Wailers, 'Scratch Perry and the Upsetter band and before that the Hippy Boys in the '60s', and some gospel records; the Ludwig the Wailers toured with was rented until Bob bought it ('Today it's in the Tuff Gong studio like a shrine'); a kit Bob bought in Delaware and gave him burned in a fire at the Green Mist in Kingston, and Bob bought him a new kit at Manny's in New York; Survival: 'One side of the LP is the Wailers, but the other side is not' (the side with Africa Unite; 'Mikey Boo played drums'); a reggae hall of fame: 'Sly Dunbar and Lloyd Nibbs. And then Hugh Malcom and Winston Graham of Soul Vendors. And one more—Carlton Barrett'; 'You once told me Ludwig and Rogers were the drumkits you preferred'; Yamaha gave him a kit on the Wailers' first visit to Japan.

title: Jas Obrecht, 'Interview with Aston "Family Man" Barrett', Ann Arbor, 14 February 2011 (transcript PDF, Legendary Reggae)
notes: Asked whether Carly invented the one-drop beat: 'Accurate. That's da man.' How: 'we in-graft that kind of Nyabinghi communal and mix it with the Jamaica mento and then we decide to create that beat and feel it on the one-drop'. Carly began on empty paint tins: 'He make a little platform and he get some different sizes of empty paint tins ... hitting the floor with his right heel as the foot drum'; one found cymbal 'was both his crash and his after-beat hi hat'. 'That's where we lock – the drummer and the bass'; 'the drum, it is the heartbeat, and the bass, it is the backbone'. The band 'first the Hippy Boys, then The Upsetters, then the Youths Professionals'. Babylon by Bus: the first night's tape was 'too exact like the LP', so they were told to 'loosen up a little'. Between Bob, Carly and Aston 'we co-write over eleven tracks'.

title: Geoff Nicholls, 'Drum Hum', Making Music, June 1987
notes: 'Carlton Barrett defined reggae drumming all over the world'; the one drop on No Woman, No Cry, the bass drum dropping halfway through the bar; the four-to-the-bar steppers on Exodus and Jamming; 'The stumbling hi-hat figures heard on many Wailers tracks eg 'Heathen' are a Barrett trademark', giving 'a sinuous twist to the loping reggae half-time feel'; 'a characteristically high and resonant snare drum tuning', which 'gave him a penetrating rim side-stick click and a very sharp rim-shot sound'.

title: David McDavitt, 'The Drums of Carlton Barrett (Bob Marley & the Wailers)': Drums and Cym/Snare pages
notes: A fan's gear history from photographs and footage, citing Mark Miller (the Wailers' stage manager 1978-81, On the Road with Bob Marley, 2013, and a 2016 email), John Masouri's Wailing Blues (2007), Music Connection (June 1987), Santelli in Modern Drummer (July 1983) and an auction listing. Rental and studio kits 1970-79, Ludwig preferred; a Ludwig clear Vistalite rental in Boston 1978; a 1976 Ludwig (3-ply, natural finish, 22x14 bass drum, 12x8, 13x9 and 16x16 toms with their bottom heads removed, a 14x6.5 Ludwig 402 snare with a coated Ambassador), lost in the Green Mist fire about 1978; the Rainbow 1977 kit 'thought ... a rental kit in England'; Yamaha 9000 (birch) from 1979: a yellow kit given after a factory visit in Japan, and a cobalt blue kit bought at Manny's, toms 8, 10, 12, 13, 16 (and a 14 or 15), single-headed; a 402 snare even on the Yamahas, 'high & dry tuning (and sometimes playing with snares off)'; a Yamaha steel snare at Dortmund 1980; Zildjian hollow-logo cymbals, 14-inch New Beat hats, crashes of 14, 16 and 18 inches; one towel between the hats at the Rainbow, 1977; a cowbell; a half Simmons kit after Marley. Its 'Cym/Snare' page is https://carltonbarrett.weebly.com/cymsnare.html.

title: David McDavitt, 'The Drums of Carlton Barrett': Playing and Etc. pages
notes: A fan's analysis, not a transcription: the snare as a 'repeater' drum (Nyabinghi), dry 16th bounce strokes on snare or toms; few crashes, a rimshot instead; cross-stick and hi-hat figures described as clave-like; the 'and' of 4 accented with an open hat or a tom; a hat and cymbal triplet figure at phrase ends (One Love, War, Zion Train); half-bar hi-hat syncopation released by straight time (The Heathen, Crazy Baldhead, Exodus); fills only to mark a section; toms tuned high and single-headed, sometimes taped; coated Ambassador snare, black dot kick; his last session (1985) on Simmons drums with Robbie Shakespeare; the Etc. page: he helped write War and Them Belly Full and helped on Who the Cap Fit and the mixes (Masouri); the 1974 Island contract unsigned by the Barretts; half of Survival made without them.

title: LargeUp, 'Toppa Top 10: Reggae's Ten Greatest Drummers' (No. 3, Carlton Barrett), 29 April 2014
notes: No byline. The Wailers' studio and touring drummer with his brother; first with Lee Perry's Upsetters; popularised the one drop rather than inventing it; complex triplet hi-hat variations (Running Away); a dry-tuned kit, a tight, high-pitched snare; timbales.

title: Howard Campbell, 'Sly Dunbar and Carlton Barrett among 100 most influential drummers', Jamaica Observer, 21 February 2015
notes: Reports totaldrumsets.com's '100 Most Influential Drummers Ever' list, and quotes it: 'Carlton's distinctive broken triplet hi-hat style was copied wholesale by The Police drummer Stewart Copeland'. Says Barrett made the 'One Drop sound (originated by Winston Grennan)' famous.

title: bonedo.de, 'Rolling Stone Magazine veröffentlicht Liste der 100 wichtigsten Drummer', 6 July 2016
notes: Lists Carlton Barrett, Bob Marley and the Wailers, at No. 29 on Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Drummers of All Time (2016). Rolling Stone's own page redirected to a paywall and was not read.

title: The Upsetters - Wikipedia
notes: The core Upsetters: Aston Barrett (bass), Carlton Barrett (drums), Alva Lewis (guitar), Glen Adams (organ), 'the studio band that is most associated with the name' and the nucleus of Bob Marley's Wailers; the Hippy Boys recruited for a UK tour; under Perry the band 'backed Bob Marley on a full-time basis, especially on the albums Soul Rebels and Soul Revolution Part II'; 'By 1972 the Barrett brothers had joined the Wailers'.

title: The Wailers (thewailers.com), Carlton Barrett biography
notes: With Aston, the rhythm on 'over 90 per cent' of Marley's Island songs; they first recorded with the Wailers for Lee Perry: Mr Brown, Duppy Conqueror, Soul Rebel; murdered in 1987 at 36.

title: Legendary Reggae, 'Feel It in the One Drop', 23 October 2011
notes: Carly and Aston 'would practice endlessly on the famous ska tunes of the day'; a long run of instrumentals with the Upsetters; 'popularizing the one drop rhythm, a percussive drumming style created by Winston Grennan'; Keith Hudson's Pick-A-Dub with Carly and Family Man; 'drum fills often do not end with a climactic cymbal'.

title: Adam Osmianski, 'Groove Transcription: Carlton Barrett, "Three Little Birds"', That Drum Blog, 15 October 2025
notes: Text only read (the notation is an image): 'a lot of subtlety going on with each bar varying ever so slightly, particularly with regards to how many notes he's playing on the hi-hat'; 'sometimes you'll hear 1e&a, while other times only 1&a'; 'There are NO crashes. None.'; 'Use open hi-hats instead'.

title: Catch a Fire - Wikipedia
notes: Island, 13 April 1973; recorded May to October 1972 at Dynamic Sound, Harry J's and Randy's, Kingston, on eight-track (Sylvan Morris); overdubbed and remixed by Chris Blackwell in London. Carlton 'Carlie' Barrett, drums (the only kit drummer credited); Aston Barrett bass (Robbie Shakespeare on Concrete Jungle and Stir It Up); Bunny Wailer bongos and conga; Alvin 'Seeco' Patterson akete. Christgau: the Barrett brothers' bass and drums 'save those that aren't from limbo'.

title: Burnin' (Bob Marley and the Wailers album) - Wikipedia
notes: Island, 19 October 1973; Harry J's, Kingston; Chris Blackwell and the Wailers producing. Carlton 'Carlie' Barrett, drums (the only drummer credited); Aston Barrett bass and the extra lead guitar on I Shot the Sheriff; Bunny Wailer percussion. Get Up, Stand Up; I Shot the Sheriff; Burnin' and Lootin'; Small Axe; Duppy Conqueror.

title: Natty Dread - Wikipedia
notes: Island, 25 October 1974; Harry J, Kingston. Carlton Barrett, drums and percussion; co-writer (with Leon Cogill) of Them Belly Full (But We Hungry) and Talkin' Blues; Aston Barrett bass; Al Anderson lead guitar; the I-Threes. Lively Up Yourself, No Woman, No Cry, Rebel Music.

title: Live! (Bob Marley and the Wailers album) - Wikipedia
notes: Island, 5 December 1975; the Lyceum Theatre, London, 17 and 18 July 1975, on the Rolling Stones Mobile. Carlton Barrett drums, Aston Barrett bass, Tyrone Downie keyboards, Al Anderson guitar, Alvin 'Seeco' Patterson percussion. Trenchtown Rock, Burnin' and Lootin', Them Belly Full, Lively Up Yourself, No Woman, No Cry, I Shot the Sheriff, Get Up, Stand Up.

title: Rastaman Vibration - Wikipedia
notes: Island, 30 April 1976; Harry J and Joe Gibbs, Kingston, mixed at Criteria, Miami. Carlton Barrett drums (no other drummer listed); co-writer of Who the Cap Fit (with Aston) and War (with Allan Cole); the credits are disputed. Crazy Baldhead, Positive Vibration, Roots, Rock, Reggae.

title: Exodus (Bob Marley and the Wailers album) - Wikipedia
notes: Island, 3 June 1977; recorded 1976 and January to April 1977 at Harry J and Island Studios, London. Carlton Barrett drums; Aston Barrett basses; Junior Marvin guitars; Tyrone Downie keyboards; Alvin 'Seeco' Patterson percussion. Rolling Stone: 'the magnificent rhythm section of Aston Barrett, bass, and Carlton Barrett, drums'. The live set recorded at the Rainbow Theatre that week (1, 3 and 4 June 1977).

title: Kaya (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Island/Tuff Gong, 23 March 1978; recorded January to April 1977 at Island Studios, London, with the Exodus sessions. Carlton Barrett drums and percussion; Winston Grennan drums (tracks not given); Alvin 'Seeco' Patterson percussion. Easy Skanking, Is This Love, Sun Is Shining, Satisfy My Soul, Running Away.

title: Survival (Bob Marley and the Wailers album) - Wikipedia
notes: 2 October 1979; Tuff Gong Studio, Kingston, January to February 1979; produced with Alex Sadkin. Carlton Barrett drums and percussion; Carlton 'Santa' Davis drums on Africa Unite; Mikey 'Boo' Richards drums on Wake Up and Live; Earl 'Chinna' Smith rhythm guitar and percussion on One Drop.

title: Uprising (Bob Marley and the Wailers album) - Wikipedia
notes: 10 June 1980; Tuff Gong, Kingston, January to April 1980. Carlton Barrett drums and percussion; Carlton 'Santa' Davis drums (tracks not given). Could You Be Loved, Zion Train, Coming In from the Cold, Redemption Song. The Uprising Tour, 1980.

title: Soul Rebels - Wikipedia
notes: Trojan, December 1970; Randy's (Studio 17), Kingston, August to November 1970; produced by Lee 'Scratch' Perry; 'sparse and haunting', no horns. The page gives no personnel.

title: King Tubbys Meets Rockers Uptown - Wikipedia
notes: Augustus Pablo and King Tubby, 1976; sessions 1972 to 1975 at Randy's, mixed at King Tubby's. Drums: Carlton 'Carlie' Barrett; bass Robbie Shakespeare and Aston Barrett; guitar Earl 'Chinna' Smith. Mostly remixes of Pablo's earlier rhythms and re-cuts of Studio One rhythms.
